blocks.content: The first five minutes of an LLD interview quietly decide the next forty. Before you design a single class, you must understand exactly what you are being asked to build, and interviewers watch closely to see if you do.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974112831-586250852.png

Prompts are vague on purpose. "Design a parking lot" could mean a tiny home garage or a sprawling airport structure. Your job is to turn that fog into a clear, agreed scope before touching any design.
Clarifying is not a delay or a stalling tactic. It is the most senior thing you can do at the start, and it is the difference between building the right system and beautifully building the wrong one.

blocks.title: Why this lesson is first among the steps
blocks.content: Every later step, entities, relationships, patterns, depends on knowing the scope. Get this wrong and everything built on top is wrong too.
1. Why Clarification Matters So Much
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972203237-406985642.png
blocks.alt: Clarifying leads to the right system, skipping leads to the wrong one

blocks.content: Design the wrong thing perfectly and you still fail the interview. Clarifying protects you from that fate.

["It stops you wasting time on features nobody asked for.","It shows maturity, because real engineers never build blindly.","It gives you the exact list of things your classes must support.","It shrinks a scary open prompt into a small, defined problem.","It builds rapport, showing the interviewer you collaborate."]
items: It stops you wasting time on features nobody asked for.
It shows maturity, because real engineers never build blindly.
It gives you the exact list of things your classes must support.
It shrinks a scary open prompt into a small, defined problem.
It builds rapport, showing the interviewer you collaborate.

blocks.content: A problem well stated is a problem half solved. The first minutes spent making the problem clear pay back many times over.
Functional vs Non Functional Requirements
Requirements come in two flavours, and a strong candidate teases out both.

{"headers":["Type","Question it answers","Examples"],"rows":[["Functional","What must the system do?","Park a car, issue a ticket, calculate a fee"],["Non functional","How well must it do it?","Handle many gates, be easy to extend"]]}
In LLD, functional requirements shape your classes and methods directly. Non functional ones, especially extensibility, shape how flexible your design needs to be.
Functional requirements, in detail
These are the concrete behaviours. For a parking lot: accept a vehicle, assign a spot, issue a ticket, compute the fee on exit. Each one usually maps to a method.
Non functional requirements, in detail

These are qualities, not features. In an LLD setting they usually mean things like "it should be easy to add new vehicle types" or "pricing rules will change often". These hints tell you where to build in flexibility.
2. The Questions to Always Ask
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972205137-528147394.png
blocks.alt: The key clarifying questions to ask

blocks.content: Keep a mental checklist of clarifying questions that fit almost any prompt. You will not ask all of them, but they prime your thinking.

["What are the core features that must work?","Who are the users or actors interacting with the system?","What is explicitly out of scope for this session?","Are there rules or constraints, like pricing, limits, or capacity?","Should the design anticipate future features, or is this a fixed set?","What are the main actions, the verbs, the system performs?"]
items: What are the core features that must work?
Who are the users or actors interacting with the system?
What is explicitly out of scope for this session?
Are there rules or constraints, like pricing, limits, or capacity?
Should the design anticipate future features, or is this a fixed set?
What are the main actions, the verbs, the system performs?

blocks.title: A pro move
blocks.content: After asking, repeat the scope back: "So we are building X, with features A, B, and C, and skipping D. Is that right?" This one sentence confirms alignment out loud.
Identify the Actors
Ask who uses the system. Each type of user, called an actor, has different needs, and those needs become features.

blocks.title: Actors in a parking lot
blocks.text: A driver enters and parks. An admin configures spots and pricing. An operator handles the gate. Each actor implies different operations your design must support.

blocks.content: Listing actors early prevents a common miss: designing only for one user and forgetting the admin or operator side entirely.
3. Turn Requirements Into Use Cases
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972206711-379192180.png
blocks.alt: Requirements become use cases become methods

blocks.content: Once features and actors are clear, translate them into concrete use cases, the specific actions the system supports. These become the methods on your classes.
This bridge from words to methods keeps your later design grounded. Every method should trace back to a real use case you agreed on.
4. Scoping to a Minimum Viable Design
blocks.text: 4. Scoping to a Minimum Viable Design

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972208562-757514972.png
blocks.alt: Split features into a core MVP and out of scope

blocks.content: You cannot design everything in forty five minutes, and you are not expected to. Agree on a minimum viable version first, then extend if time allows.

blocks.title: Scoping a food delivery app
blocks.text: Core: place an order, assign an agent, track status. Out of scope for now: payments, ratings, promotions. Agreeing this keeps the design focused and finishable.

blocks.content: Explicitly parking features as "out of scope for now" is powerful. It shows you can prioritise, and it protects your limited time.
You are not judged on how many features you cram in. You are judged on how cleanly you design the ones that matter.
5. Stating Assumptions
When the interviewer is vague and you must move on, state an assumption out loud and continue. This keeps momentum while staying honest.
A clear assumption is far better than a silent guess. If the interviewer disagrees, they correct you, and you have lost nothing.

blocks.title: Say it, do not hide it
blocks.content: Every assumption you make silently is a risk. Every assumption you state is a chance for the interviewer to align with you.
6. Defining the Boundaries
Good clarification also draws the edges of the system: what it does, and what it deliberately leaves to something else.
["What does the system own, and what does it not?","Where does another system take over, like payments?","What inputs arrive from outside, and what does it output?"]
items: What does the system own, and what does it not?
Where does another system take over, like payments?
What inputs arrive from outside, and what does it output?

blocks.content: Clear boundaries stop your design from sprawling into every related feature. You design a parking lot, not the entire city.
7. A Worked Clarification Dialogue
Here is how a strong clarification sounds, compressed into a short back and forth.

blocks.title: The dialogue
blocks.text: You: Is this a single level or multi level lot? Interviewer: Multi level. You: Different vehicle sizes? Interviewer: Yes, bikes, cars, trucks. You: How is pricing decided? Interviewer: Hourly for now. You: So multi level, three sizes, hourly pricing, no passes yet. I will design for that.

blocks.content: In four questions, a vague prompt became a precise problem. That is the entire goal of this step.
8. Clarifying Data and Constraints
Beyond features, ask about the data and the rules that govern it. These constraints often shape your classes more than the features do.

["What are the limits, like maximum capacity or maximum users?","Are there rules about pricing, timing, or validation?","What data must the system store for each entity?","Are there states an entity moves through, like free, occupied, reserved?"]
items: What are the limits, like maximum capacity or maximum users?
Are there rules about pricing, timing, or validation?
What data must the system store for each entity?
Are there states an entity moves through, like free, occupied, reserved?

blocks.title: Constraints in a parking lot
blocks.text: A spot fits only certain vehicle types. A ticket has an entry time used for pricing. A lot has a fixed capacity per level. Each constraint becomes a field or a rule in your design.

blocks.content: Surfacing constraints early prevents nasty surprises later, like discovering halfway that pricing depends on data you never captured.
9. A Word on Scale
LLD is mostly about clean class design, not massive distributed scale. Still, a light question about scale can guide your choices.

Ask whether the system is one instance or many, and whether numbers are small or large. You are not designing servers here, but knowing that there could be many parking lots hints that you may want a manager class above a single lot.

blocks.title: Keep scale light
blocks.content: Do not turn an LLD interview into a system design one. A single sentence about scale is enough. The focus stays on classes and responsibilities.
10. The Order to Ask Your Questions
blocks.text: 10. The Order to Ask Your Questions

blocks.content: Random questions feel scattered. A simple order makes you sound structured and in control.

["Start with the core features: what must it do?","Then the actors: who uses it?","Then the constraints: what rules and limits apply?","Then the scope: what is out of scope for now?","Finish by repeating the agreed scope back for confirmation."]
items: Start with the core features: what must it do?
Then the actors: who uses it?
Then the constraints: what rules and limits apply?
Then the scope: what is out of scope for now?
Finish by repeating the agreed scope back for confirmation.

blocks.content: This order moves from the big picture down to the details, which is exactly how a senior engineer thinks through a new problem.
11. A Second Example: Designing an Elevator
blocks.text: 11. A Second Example: Designing an Elevator

blocks.content: To prove the questions are universal, apply them to a different prompt: design an elevator system.

blocks.title: Clarifying an elevator
blocks.text: How many elevators and floors? Who requests, riders inside and people on floors? What decides which elevator answers a call? Is there a rule for idle behaviour? In four questions the prompt is concrete.

blocks.content: ["Features: request a floor, move up and down, open and close doors.","Actors: a rider inside, a person waiting on a floor.","Constraints: capacity, direction rules, idle position."]
items: Features: request a floor, move up and down, open and close doors.
Actors: a rider inside, a person waiting on a floor.
Constraints: capacity, direction rules, idle position.

blocks.content: The exact same clarifying pattern turned a second vague prompt into a clear problem. That is why this step is a universal skill, not a parking lot trick.
12. Building the Requirements List
As you clarify, write a short list on the board. This becomes your contract, and you can check every class you design against it.
A visible list keeps you and the interviewer aligned, and it stops you from quietly drifting away from the agreed scope as the design grows.
13. From Requirements to a Design Plan
blocks.text: 13. From Requirements to a Design Plan

blocks.content: Clarification is not the end, it is the launch pad. Once the list is agreed, you can name the entities, sketch the relationships, and begin designing with confidence.
Everything downstream, the classes, the relationships, the patterns, is only as good as the requirements you started from.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Ask before assuming","Confirm scope out loud","Separate must have from nice to have","State assumptions clearly","List the actors and use cases"],"cons":["Designing on a silent guess","Trying to build every feature","Ignoring constraints and limits","Asking twenty aimless questions","Forgetting non functional needs"]}
15. Common Questions
How many questions is too many? - Ask enough to define the scope, usually a focused handful. Endless aimless questions are as bad as asking none.
What if the interviewer says you decide? - Make a reasonable choice, state it as an assumption, and move on. They are testing your judgement.
Do non functional requirements matter in LLD? - Yes, lightly. Hints like "it should be easy to add new types" directly guide how flexible your classes should be.
Should I write the requirements down? - Yes, a short list on the board keeps you and the interviewer aligned and gives you something to check your design against.
16. Key Takeaways

["Never design before you understand the problem.","Separate functional from non functional requirements.","Identify the actors and turn features into concrete use cases.","Agree a minimum viable scope, and park the rest as out of scope for now.","State assumptions out loud instead of guessing silently.","Repeat the scope back to confirm alignment."]
items: Never design before you understand the problem.
Separate functional from non functional requirements.
Identify the actors and turn features into concrete use cases.
Agree a minimum viable scope, and park the rest as out of scope for now.
State assumptions out loud instead of guessing silently.
Repeat the scope back to confirm alignment.

blocks.title: The golden habit
blocks.content: Spend the first few minutes clarifying, every single time. It is the cheapest, highest value habit in the entire interview.
Clarify, confirm, then design. That order alone puts you ahead of most candidates.
Nail this step and the whole interview flows. With a clear, agreed scope in hand, you are ready to find the entities that will become your classes.
